props.title: Yesterday
props.initialSlug: Tragic romance unfolds across Korean border tensions

sections.content: Yesterday (2004) stands as a landmark in South African cinema, marking the first feature film ever produced in the Zulu language. Director Darrell Roodt crafts an intimate portrait of HIV/AIDS in rural South Africa through the story of a mother determined to survive long enough to see her daughter start school. The film's power lies in its simplicity and universality, following similar thematic threads to other acclaimed HIV/AIDS narratives like Philadelphia (1993) and Dallas Buyers Club (2013), but through an essential African perspective.

sections.content: The film sparked a wave of African cinema addressing the AIDS crisis with remarkable sensitivity. Tsotsi (2005) touched on similar themes of parenthood in crisis, while Life, Above All (2010) expanded on Yesterday's exploration of community stigma and resilience. These films share Roodt's approach of using intimate personal stories to illuminate broader social issues, much like And the Band Played On (1993) did for the American AIDS crisis.

Yesterday's influence extends beyond its HIV/AIDS narrative, helping establish a new visual language for rural African storytelling. The film's gorgeous landscapes and naturalistic performances influenced later works like The First Grader (2010) and Queen of Katwe (2016). Its success paved the way for more indigenous language films, challenging Hollywood's dominance in telling African stories. SUBHEAD: Impact on Global Health Cinema

sections.content: The film's approach to health advocacy through storytelling created a template followed by films like 93 Days (2016) about the Ebola crisis and Fire in the Blood (2013) examining pharmaceutical access in developing nations. Yesterday's success demonstrated how medical issues could be explored through deeply personal narratives without sacrificing cultural authenticity or dramatic impact.
